title: Credit Score Prediction
description: Developed and benchmarked multiclass credit-score classifiers on 25,000 initial customer-month records, comparing 8 model/feature-set combinations. The selected XGBoost model reached 0.6898 macro F1 and 70.79% accuracy on a 4,577-row group-disjoint evaluation set.
problemStatement: Predict customer credit-score categories (Good, Poor, and Standard) from financial behavior and credit history. Compare four machine learning algorithms and two feature-set strategies using customer-disjoint splitting and macro-averaged metrics.
businessContext: Credit scoring is a multiclass risk categorization task. This academic study explores how supervised learning may help analysts organize credit-risk patterns. It is not a validated lending decision system or a substitute for appropriate financial and fairness reviews.
dataset: Credit-score customer-month dataset (data_C.csv): 25,000 original observations and 29 columns including customer profile, credit facilities, loan details, repayment behavior, balances, and the Credit_Score target. After cleaning and filtering, the notebook reports 22,412 modeling records. Personal identifiers (Name, SSN, ID) are not model predictors.
datasetSize: 25,000 original records (29 columns) · 22,412 after cleaning · 17,835 train / 4,577 test · 3 classes
preprocessing: Audited missing values, inconsistent numeric/text formatting, duplicates and financial-value anomalies across 29 original columns.
Repaired inconsistent age and credit-related values, applied customer-based data consistency checks, and retained 22,412 records after documented cleaning.
Used StratifiedGroupKFold with Customer_ID as the group variable: 7,212 train customers and 1,830 test customers with zero overlapping customers.
Constructed sklearn Pipelines and ColumnTransformers: numerical median imputation, categorical most-frequent imputation and one-hot encoding; RobustScaler for the linear-model branch.
Excluded names, social security numbers and customer identifiers from the final classification features.
featureEngineering: Experiment A — Original + Feature Engineering (32 features): constructed EMI-, investment-, balance- and debt-to-salary ratios; credit-history missingness; nine loan-type flags; and spending/payment categories.
Experiment B — Original + Loan Flags (31 features): kept 17 numerical, 5 categorical and 9 binary loan-type features; this was the best-performing feature configuration.
Encoded loan categories such as mortgage, student, payday, auto, personal and debt-consolidation loans into model-ready binary flags.
methodology: Trained and tuned four algorithms — Logistic Regression, Random Forest, XGBoost and LightGBM — on both feature-set strategies (8 total trained/evaluated combinations).
For the engineered-feature comparison, used RandomizedSearchCV with 20 candidates and 5 stratified group-aware CV folds per algorithm, optimizing macro F1.
For the original-plus-loan-flags comparison, used RandomizedSearchCV with 10 candidates and 3 group-aware CV folds per algorithm, optimizing macro F1.
Used customer-disjoint train/test partitions (17,835 / 4,577 rows); tested all models with accuracy, balanced accuracy, macro precision/recall/F1 and multiclass one-vs-rest ROC-AUC.

Selected the final saved XGBoost configuration based on the notebook-reported test macro-F1 across the two feature sets; the associated final estimate should therefore be treated as exploratory rather than an independently confirmed holdout result.
results: Best recorded configuration: XGBoost with Original + Loan Flags (31 predictors); test macro F1 = 0.6898, accuracy = 70.79%, balanced accuracy = 0.7040, macro OvR ROC-AUC = 0.8591.
XGBoost using Original + Feature Engineering achieved macro F1 = 0.6860 and accuracy = 70.44%; both feature configurations outperformed Logistic Regression on macro F1.
Evaluated all 8 algorithm/feature-set combinations on the 4,577-row test partition; highest recorded macro F1 = 0.6898.
Verified zero Customer_ID overlap between train and test (7,212 vs. 1,830 customers); saved the selected pipeline and label encoder to a Joblib model artifact.
Best XGBoost confusion-matrix diagonal: 566 Good, 896 Poor, and 1,778 Standard predictions correctly classified.
insights: Using original numerical/categorical credit variables plus explicit loan-type flags slightly outperformed the more extensively engineered ratio-feature strategy on macro F1.
The dominant Standard class (13,282 of the original 25,000 records) makes macro-averaged metrics more informative than overall accuracy alone.
Group-based splitting is important because monthly observations may refer to the same customer; this split avoids customer overlap across train and test.
A comparison of class-level confusion matrices provides more context than accuracy alone, particularly for the Good and Poor categories.
businessImpact: Potential decision support for exploratory customer credit-risk segmentation and analyst-led case prioritization. Any regulated or production credit decision would require independent validation, calibration, explainability, bias/fairness checks, legal review and monitoring.
challenges: Correcting malformed numerical values and anomalous financial fields while preserving plausible credit-risk variation.
Handling repeated customer-month observations without customer overlap in evaluation.
Comparing linear and tree-based models under mixed numerical/categorical feature types and a nonuniform class distribution.
limitations: Reported metrics are sourced from the supplied notebook and have not been independently reproduced in this documentation.
The final algorithm/feature-set was chosen using test-set macro F1; a new untouched holdout or outer group-aware validation is needed for unbiased final model selection and evaluation.
Dataset cleaning occurred before the train/test split, so some preprocessing steps warrant an additional leakage audit and migration into a train-fitted pipeline.
The source dataset contains personally identifying fields and is intentionally not redistributed in the public GitHub package.
An end-to-end deployment of this specific credit-score artifact has not been confirmed from the four files supplied here.
futureImprovements: Introduce an independent final group holdout (or nested grouped cross-validation), keeping model selection away from final test data.
Place all learned data-cleaning statistics within train-fitted pipeline stages for leakage-safe reproducibility.
Add calibrated class probabilities, group-wise error analysis, model explainability, and fairness checks before any production-oriented use.
Document separate Streamlit / MLflow / AWS deployment evidence once the implementation files are provided.

title: Bank Marketing Campaign Classification
projectType: Group academic final project — Machine Learning (LA09, 4 contributors)
status: Completed group modeling experiment; notebook and poster verified
description: Collaborative classification study of 41,188 bank campaign records, comparing six models and class-imbalance strategies to prioritize likely term-deposit subscribers. Tuned Logistic Regression recorded 0.6979 cross-validated positive-class precision; held-out positive-class precision was approximately 0.67.
problemStatement: Predict whether a bank customer will subscribe to a term deposit (yes/no), with the modeling objective centered on precision for the positive (yes) class to support selective telemarketing outreach.
businessContext: The academic team examined how campaign response prediction could guide prospect prioritization and call-center resource allocation. The study reports exploratory metrics and does not claim a measured increase in real-world conversion or cost savings.
dataset: Bank Marketing — bank-additional-full.csv from the public Bank Marketing dataset linked in the original group notebook. The source has 41,188 rows and 21 variables: demographics, prior/current contact attributes, macroeconomic context, and binary response target y. The modeling notebook retained 40,184 rows and 20 columns after dropping default, removing duplicates, and filtering missing housing/loan fields.
datasetSize: 41,188 initial customer-contact records · 40,184 cleaned · 8,037 test observations · yes: 4,532 (11.28%) / no: 35,652 (88.72%) after cleaning
preprocessing: Converted categorical unknown markers to missing values; inspected six affected columns (job, marital, education, default, housing, loan).

Dropped the default feature following the group’s recorded chi-square investigation, removed 14 duplicated records, filled selected categorical unknown values as others, and removed observations missing housing or loan.
Encoded categorical features using one-hot encoding for selected fields and binary encoding for job, education, month and day_of_week through ColumnTransformer.
Created an 80/20 train–test split with random_state=100; the original notebook did not specify stratification for this split.
Excluded duration from the predictive feature set because call duration is not available before a telemarketing contact concludes.
featureEngineering: Constructed a categorical encoding pipeline combining OneHotEncoder and category_encoders.BinaryEncoder.
Compared training configurations without resampling, with RandomOverSampler and with RandomUnderSampler inside modeling pipelines.
Examined logistic regression coefficient magnitudes of transformed predictors; encoded month and contact features were prominent in the notebook output.
methodology: Conducted exploratory data analysis of target prevalence, employment-related macroeconomic attributes, previous contacts, job categories, marital status, education and communication channels.
Benchmarked Logistic Regression, KNN, Decision Tree, Random Forest, XGBoost and SVM with five-fold StratifiedKFold cross-validation, using positive-class precision as the benchmark score.
Compared baseline, random oversampling and random undersampling approaches within pipelines to assess the effect of imbalance handling on precision.
Selected Logistic Regression as the precision-oriented candidate, then ran RandomizedSearchCV with 100 parameter candidates × 5 CV folds (500 fits) on the training set.
Evaluated the tuned classifier on a held-out test set (8,037 rows) with per-class precision, recall, F1 and accuracy; inspected coefficients for encoded feature interpretation.
Preserved original group notebook output and figures; figures in this case study include original notebook plots and a chart derived directly from its recorded CV scores.
evaluationMetrics: Stratified 5-fold CV mean precision and standard deviation
results: Cleaned 41,188 original observations to 40,184 rows; target yes: 4,532 (11.28%), no: 35,652 (88.72%).
Six-model baseline five-fold CV precision ranking: Logistic Regression 0.6826, SVM 0.6391, XGBoost 0.5891, Random Forest 0.5507, KNN 0.5218, Decision Tree 0.3049 (from the notebook benchmark output).
Tuning Logistic Regression with RandomizedSearchCV increased mean cross-validated positive-class precision from 0.6826 to 0.6979 (+1.53 percentage points across the recorded experiments).
Tuned Logistic Regression test report: 8,037 samples (905 yes / 7,132 no); yes-class precision ≈ 0.67, recall ≈ 0.18, F1 ≈ 0.28, and overall accuracy ≈ 0.90.
Baseline comparisons included RandomOverSampler and RandomUnderSampler; neither resampled Logistic Regression configuration achieved the recorded no-resampling precision.
Original notebook visualizations analyze customer contact channels, jobs and demographic patterns; group poster documents the four collaborators.
insights: Precision is relevant for reducing unsuccessful outreach among predicted positives; however, at 0.18 recall the tuned model identifies only about 18% of actual subscribers, limiting campaign coverage.
The post-cleaning target is strongly imbalanced: about 11.28% yes, so 90% overall accuracy alone is not sufficient to judge value for finding subscribers.
Original EDA found higher observed conversion among certain contact channels and customer categories, but those associations are descriptive rather than evidence of causal uplift.
Call duration was analyzed for historical patterns but excluded from model inputs, consistent with trying to score customers before a call.
The group’s poster provides a shorter result summary; the more precise tuned CV metric (0.6979) comes from the final notebook output.
businessImpact: Academic prototype for ranking potential term-deposit prospects and discussing telemarketing efficiency. No production pilot, observed ROI, or realized bank conversion uplift is claimed.
challenges: Managing unknown categorical values, duplicate bank contacts and differing data types in the preprocessing pipeline.
Balancing outreach precision against low positive-class recall under substantial class imbalance.
Comparing resampling strategies and six classifiers before selecting a precision-oriented approach.
limitations: The result is group work by four students; individual technical contributions were not specified, so no exclusive ownership is claimed.
At the recorded operating threshold, test recall for the yes class is approximately 0.18 despite 0.67 precision: most true subscribers would not be identified.

Some cleaning and exploratory feature selection were conducted before the train–test split; the feature-selection step and preprocessing should be audited for potential leakage and reworked as train-fitted steps for production evaluation.
Several optimization runs in the notebook emit convergence warnings, and no reproducibility run has been performed in this packaging step.
No real campaign A/B test, production deployment, calibrated uplift model or realized telemarketing cost reduction was provided.
The group poster uses a different rounded CV precision snapshot from the final saved notebook; this case study uses the final notebook outputs.
futureImprovements: Tune decision thresholds according to business contact capacity and compare precision-recall curves, average precision and captured-positive volume.
Run nested or fully train-fitted preprocessing/feature selection with a stratified held-out test and reproducible random seeds.
Use cost-sensitive evaluation and outreach simulation to assess campaign value without asserting hypothetical savings as measured outcomes.
Add probability calibration and temporal validation against later bank marketing periods.

title: SPARC 2026 Finalist — Customer Repeat-Order Analytics
projectType: SPARC 2026 Data Science Competition — Finalist (3-member team)
description: SPARC 2026 finalist entry by a three-person team, centered on exploratory analysis and data preparation of 319,978 vehicle-sales transactions. Investigated duplicates, inconsistent customer records, demographic anomalies, geographic categories, product information and financing-data quality.
problemStatement: Explore historical vehicle sales and financing records to understand customer-transaction patterns and prepare trustworthy data for repeat-order analysis and customer follow-up prioritization.
businessContext: Competition: SPARC 2026. Team: Anang Tantowi, Hazel Novero Winata and Junico (team name: Trio Tunggal). The team reached the finalist stage. This public case study intentionally presents EDA and preprocessing work, rather than predictive-model scores, source code or purported commercial outcomes.
dataset: Historical vehicle-sales / financing transactions described in the team presentation: 319,978 initial transaction rows and 28 features spanning customer identifiers and demographics, motorbike products, dealers and geography, prices and financing details, payment methods, and dates. One row represents one transaction, not one unique customer; the EDA reports 266,927 distinct Customer_ID values.
datasetSize: 319,978 initial transactions · 28 features · 266,927 customer IDs (reported) · 317,637 rows after exact deduplication
preprocessing: Identified and removed 2,341 fully duplicated rows (319,978 → 317,637). Crucially, distinct transactions from the same customer were not treated as duplicate records because repeat activity is central to the study.
Validated customer identifiers against the documented CUST-XXXX format, excluding blank identifiers and aggregate TOTAL records that do not represent actual individual transactions.
Standardized payment-method codes (1 = cash; 2 = credit) and examined Finance Company values, including the special N category, before interpreting financing-related fields.

Audited malformed ages, with recorded values reaching 1,230 years. The presentation describes recomputing age from birth dates and retaining plausible ages from 17 to 90, rather than trusting unvalidated numeric age fields.

Assessed high-cardinality and inconsistent geographical fields. Removed Kelurahan, Kode POS and Wilayah from the selected feature set; retained Kecamatan after uppercase normalization, punctuation/space cleanup, and grouping categories with five or fewer records into OTHER.
Normalized dealer-area naming (including PPU = Penajam Paser Utara), treated numeric-looking dealer identifiers as categories, and reviewed the distribution of seven primary dealer regions.
Standardized vehicle-product categories such as Type Series, Segment, motorcycle model codes and colors; reviewed manufacturing-year values and filtered implausible years as described in the slides.
Converted heterogeneous money strings (such as Rp 2.056.000 and unformatted numbers) into numeric down-payment and installment fields; documented the derived fields dp_aktual_clean and cicilan_clean.

Compared cleaned down payments with On-the-Road (OTR) prices through dp_ratio = dp_aktual_clean / OTR. The slides report 65,103 credit transactions where down payment exceeded the vehicle price; these were flagged and excluded under the team’s documented business rule.
Reviewed tenor values and missingness. The presentation describes restricting selected financing records to tenors of 1–3 and identifying constant payment-method categories after filtering.
Rechecked residual missingness, notably Tgl Cetak and DLR Group at approximately 96% each in a later processing stage, before deciding which fields were usable for downstream analysis.

Reviewed statistical outliers in OTR, down payment and installment amounts using domain checks rather than indiscriminate deletion; the team presentation describes log transforming skewed price information.
featureEngineering: Geographical category normalization and rare-category consolidation for Kecamatan to reduce inconsistent labels and sparsity.
Numeric extraction of monetary values and a down-payment-to-vehicle-price ratio for transaction validation.
Categorical correction for dealer identifiers, motorbike product codes and sales-location labels.

Chronological customer-transaction grouping to distinguish one-time from repeat customers in a retrospective analysis; the presentation defines a repeat customer as one with more than one recorded transaction.
methodology: Data understanding: distinguished transaction records from unique customers, mapped the 28 original fields and checked sample distributions of age, payment method, vehicle price, dealership and product categories.
Numerical EDA: reviewed ranges, central tendency, right-skewed prices, zero values, age anomalies and unusual financial amounts requiring business validation.
Categorical EDA: explored customer identifiers, gender/other demographic attributes, geography, dealer regions, vehicle series, segment, color and credit-related categories.
Data quality audit: checked exact duplicates, invalid identifiers, inconsistent types and text, long-tailed geographic labels, hidden missing values, financing mismatches, and anomalous dates.

Preprocessing documentation: explained deduplication, normalization, targeted filtering, value-type conversion, category grouping, ratio checks and missingness reviews through original presentation slides.
Competition presentation: organized the findings and preprocessing decisions into a team case study that reached the finalist stage of SPARC 2026.
insights: The distinction between records and unique customers matters: 319,978 transactions correspond to a reported 266,927 distinct customer identifiers, so repeated customer IDs should not be dropped as if they were exact duplicate rows.
The data-quality audit identified 2,341 exact duplicate rows as well as more subtle anomalies involving age, customer identifiers, dates and monetary fields.

Geographic dimensions include numerous rare values and spelling variants. Retaining the most useful granularity while consolidating rare districts helps make descriptive segmentation more interpretable.
Vehicle prices were positively skewed; zeros and very high monetary values needed context-sensitive checks rather than automatic outlier removal.
The down-payment-to-OTR validation found concentrated inconsistencies in credit records, emphasizing the importance of testing business rules before interpreting financing patterns.
High missingness in some operational columns and imbalanced demographic categories called for cautious interpretation and further source-data checks.

A retrospective repeat-customer flag based on all recorded transactions describes historical repeat activity; prospective prediction would require a separate observation window and future outcome window to prevent temporal leakage.
businessImpact: Achieved finalist recognition at SPARC 2026 as part of a three-person team. The documented EDA and preprocessing work builds a clearer picture of transaction quality and customer behavior for a potential follow-up prioritization workflow; no quantified marketing uplift or predictive-model performance is claimed.
challenges: Distinguishing genuine repeated customer purchases from erroneous duplicate transaction rows.
Reconciling high-cardinality district labels and inconsistent formats across dealer and geographic attributes.
Handling implausible ages, nonstandard monetary strings, extensive missingness and inconsistent financing records without making unsupported assumptions.
Maintaining a meaningful customer-level analytical view from transaction-level records.
limitations: Numbers and cleaning rules in this case study are sourced from the team’s competition slide deck; the underlying customer-level dataset and code were not provided for an independent reproduction of the calculations.

The deck documents exclusion rules for unusual down-payment ratios and certain tenor values. These rules should be validated against the original data dictionary and finance-business definitions before reuse.
A full-history repeat flag is retrospective and would not by itself constitute leakage-free prospective repeat-order prediction.
No model training metrics, comparative prediction results, raw dataset or source-code repository are displayed, consistent with the scope selected for this public portfolio case study.
The source PDF also contains unrelated slides about Vision Transformers; only the relevant SPARC EDA/preprocessing slides are used here.
futureImprovements: Confirm disputed monetary and customer-identifier semantics with a formal data dictionary before applying irreversible filtering.
Document stage-by-stage row retention and field-level missingness alongside the existing cleaning decisions.
Validate temporal customer histories using a clearly specified historical observation period and a later repeat-order outcome period.
Monitor category consistency and data-quality rules across new monthly transaction batches.

title: ASA DataFest 2026 Finalist — Patient Risk Journey Clustering
projectType: ASA DataFest BINUS 2026 · Team Bismillah · Competition finalist
description: Competition finalist case study focused on large-scale healthcare data integration and patient clustering: 7,675,801 original encounters, 9,313,853 merged records, and 57,386 patient profiles with 22 engineered features. Analyzed five social-risk and patient-journey segments, including a potentially under-screened high-risk group.
problemStatement: How can millions of encounters, diagnosis records and social-determinant responses be transformed into patient-level segments that reveal different care journeys and groups warranting closer screening? The portfolio case study focuses solely on the patient-clustering portion of the team presentation.
businessContext: ASA DataFest BINUS 2026, Team Bismillah. The submitted presentation interprets five exploratory patient segments by clinical/operational journey complexity and social determinants of health. This analysis is a nonclinical, descriptive segmentation study, not a validated diagnostic or triage system.
dataset: Seven linked healthcare source tables: encounters, patients, diagnosis, departments, providers, social_determinants, and TIGER census geographic codes. The saved notebook starts from 7,675,801 encounter records, then expands to 9,313,853 rows after sequential left joins. One-to-many diagnosis and social-response joins can increase row counts; the 9.31 million joined rows are not 9.31 million unique patients or independent visits.
datasetSize: 7,675,801 base encounters → 9,313,853 joined rows → 1,275,948 rows with social-determinant coverage → 1,210,243 clustering records → 57,386 distinct patient profiles × 22 features
preprocessing: Loaded seven source CSV tables into Pandas and made separate working copies: patients, encounters, diagnosis, departments, providers, social_determinants and tigercensuscodes.

Normalized the join keys as strings: trimmed whitespace, stripped accidental trailing .0 suffixes, replaced placeholder nulls with NaN and prepared CensusBlockGroupFipsCode/GEOID for geographic joining.

Verified foreign-key matching before joining. For example, patient join coverage was 7,353,621 of 7,675,801 encounter rows, while only 83,359 encounter keys initially matched a social-determinants record.

Performed sequential left joins: encounters + patients (7,675,801 rows), + diagnosis (8,099,023), + departments and providers, + TIGER geographic reference, + social determinants (9,313,853). Checked row counts and shapes at each step.
Audited nulls and repeated EncounterKey records after the social determinant join, then narrowed the merged table to 1,275,948 rows containing social-response information.
Removed rows with missing essential patient, disease-group and social-response fields, retaining 1,210,243 records for the clustering preparation.
Mapped DisplayName + AnswerText pairs to a custom ordinal social RiskScore (0/1/2 where applicable); maintained an is_missing indicator for noninterpretable or missing responses.
Filled 223,813 missing social RiskScore entries using their respective Domain mean values, keeping the originally missing-response flag for downstream analysis.
featureEngineering: Converted encounter/social-response rows to one patient per row using PatientDurableKey as the patient-level index.
Pivoted mean RiskScore into eleven domain features including stress, social connections, physical activity, food insecurity, housing stability, financial strain, transportation needs and depression.

Aggregated eleven patient-level risk and journey indicators: average/max/min/std social risk; question count and diversity; domain diversity; unique encounter count; unique disease-group count; missing rate; and missing count.
Joined domain scores and journey indicators into a 57,386 × 22 patient-feature matrix; missing engineered values were filled before StandardScaler transformation.
Used total_encounters and unique_diseases to visualize journey complexity, while composite social-risk scores described relative differences in screening responses.
methodology: Analyzed the clustering-only workflow from healthcare data integration to five interpretive patient groups, excluding the separate readmission and physician-shortage topics in the team presentation.
Standardized 22 heterogeneous patient features with StandardScaler before computing distances for K-Means.
Compared K-Means candidates k=2 through k=8 using inertia (elbow method) and sampled silhouette evaluation (up to 5,000 patient profiles).
The saved selection table records the highest silhouette coefficient at k=5 (0.327972) versus k=4 (0.325479), motivating the five-segment solution used in the final team slide.
Profiled groups by social-determinant domains, encounter counts, number of disease groups and disease-category distribution; used PCA as an exploratory two-dimensional clustering visualization.
Presented the final five-segment Patient Risk Journey Map, contrasting encounter visibility with relative social risk and annotated disease profiles, as shown in the team presentation.

Preserved the five cluster names and numbered labels exactly as presented: Cluster 1 Low Risk, Cluster 0 Moderate, Cluster 2 High Complexity, Cluster 3 Psychosocial High Risk, Cluster 4 Hidden High Risk.
evaluationMetrics: Cluster-level descriptive social-risk and journey profiles
results: Original encounter table: 7,675,801 rows. Sequential data integration produced 9,313,853 joined rows, including row growth caused by one-to-many joins.
Social-determinant screening filter retained 1,275,948 rows; required-field cleaning retained 1,210,243 clustering records.
Patient-level feature engineering produced 57,386 unique patient profiles represented by 22 clustering features.
K-Means candidate evaluation (k=2–8) recorded its highest sampled silhouette coefficient at k=5: 0.327972.
Final competition presentation described five segments: Low Risk (1), Moderate (0), High Complexity (2), Psychosocial High Risk (3), and Hidden High Risk (4).
The competition team reached the finalist stage, as reported by the project participant; the patient-clustering map was included in the final team presentation.
insights: Cluster 1 (Low Risk): comparatively low recorded social/clinical risk and a simple documented healthcare journey; mainly suggested for preventive-care discussion.
Cluster 0 (Moderate): average relative risk with many general check-ups; exploratory opportunity for early monitoring and lifestyle support.
Cluster 2 (High Complexity): frequent encounters and multiple disease groups, suggesting a more complex care journey and a potential need for coordinated follow-up.
Cluster 3 (Psychosocial High Risk): elevated stress and social/financial burdens with mental-health disease patterns; suggests an integrated clinical-and-social perspective.
Cluster 4 (Hidden High Risk): elevated derived social-risk signals despite low encounter visibility; a hypothesis for possible under-screening, not proof that every member is clinically high risk.
The presentation's central message is that encounter utilization alone does not establish patient risk; social determinants and screening coverage add useful descriptive context.
businessImpact: Translated a multi-million-row healthcare integration workflow into interpretable population-level segmentation for the ASA DataFest finalist presentation. The proposed use is to inform further screening, outreach planning and care-coordination research; patient-level clinical benefit or causal impact has not been demonstrated.
challenges: Managing joins across seven heterogeneous healthcare tables while monitoring one-to-many row amplification and inconsistent key representations.
Reducing millions of encounter and social-response rows to a consistent patient-level unit of analysis without mistaking join-expanded rows for independent patients.
Handling numerous sparse or uninterpretable social-survey answers and making the rule-based social-risk encoding auditable.
Comparing cluster count candidates efficiently for 57,386 rows with 22 features while keeping results interpretable to nontechnical stakeholders.
limitations: This is unsupervised exploratory segmentation. The custom social-risk mapping and mean imputation are heuristic, not clinically calibrated or externally validated risk scores.

The original clustering notebook contains a saved output showing only labels 0–3 even though the code specifies best_k=5; five labels and group descriptions are therefore grounded in the final presentation and prior project discussion, not treated as validated per-cluster counts from that cached cell.
Joining diagnosis and social-response tables increases row counts through one-to-many relationships; neither 9,313,853 joined rows nor 1,210,243 records represent unique patients.
Zero-filled missing domain aggregates and domain-mean risk imputations may affect cluster distances and interpretability.
Claims about hidden high risk, psychosocial burden and under-screening are descriptive screening hypotheses, not diagnoses, causal explanations or evidence of clinical outcomes.
Competition finalist status is reported by the project participant; the presentation supplied here does not itself include an official finalist confirmation.
futureImprovements: Rerun the final k=5 segmentation end-to-end and save a consistent five-cluster profile table, counts and labeled outputs for independent verification.
Audit and document one-to-many join cardinality and examine the sensitivity of cluster memberships to risk-score coding, imputation and domain coverage.
Test stability of patient segments across alternative time windows and evaluate them with domain experts before any clinical application.

results: 100% test accuracy and F1-score of 1.000 were reported for the selected Random Forest original-feature configuration in the MLflow pipeline.

100% held-out placement classification accuracy for the selected Random Forest model within the submitted structured dataset.
Analyzed 5,000 student records across 18 variables and worked with a salary subset of 866 placed students.

insights: All 5,000 placement labels agree with a deterministic four-threshold rule (CGPA ≥ 7, technical skill ≥ 60, soft skill ≥ 55, backlogs ≤ 2).
Tree-based classifiers identify threshold splits well; this dataset structure helps explain the perfect held-out test accuracy for the selected placement model.
The regression track was evaluated separately as a continuous-outcome task, using MAE, RMSE and R² rather than classification accuracy.
Building monolithic and decoupled applications showed two ways of connecting trained models to user-facing interfaces.
businessImpact: Demonstrates an integrated student-outcome analytics prototype: from feature analysis and ML model selection to a user-facing application and reusable prediction API.
